items.title: Dan Morgenstern — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I got to know Coleman quite well... We had become friendly. ... Coleman did a very big thing for me in terms of establishing me in the musicians’ circle.

ctx.x: Why don’t you tell us about your ancestry, as much as you remember – your parents and even further back if you . . .

It’s a fairly complicated – but I’ll try to be brief. My father was born in what was then the Austro-Hungarian Empire. Between the world wars it was Poland. After World War II it became the Soviet Union, but now it’s Ukraine. So it had a scattered history. He was born into a Hassidic family, but not in what we generally think of as eastern European Jewry. We mostly think of what they call a stetl, which is a small

town or a village. This was not even a village. It was just a collection of farmhouses, a very small spot on the map. My paternal grandfather was the manager of an estate that belonged to a Polish noblewoman. So my father grew up in a rural atmosphere. Like most Jewish kids, he went to – very early on to a school where you learn to read Hebrew. So he grew up multi­ lingual: Polish, Russian, Ukrainian. His father, unlike most Hassids, wanted him to have a formal Westernized education. He said, if you don’t know…

items.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013
items.q: you had Coleman Hawkins once in a while... Freddie... said that Coleman Hawkins was wrapping packages in Queens. Coleman Hawkins first of all never went near Queens...

ctx.x: Well you must have been on your way to becoming pretty hip yourself, even maybe you didn’t even realize it.

I had no thoughts at that time of becoming in any way professionally involved in the music, but I was — it was like 52nd Street was in its final stages, but it was still alive and it was no small thing to have Sidney Bechet at Jimmy Ryan’s and across the street maybe Charlie Parker if you were lucky and he was in town. And, you know, Billie Holiday at the Onyx Club. So there was still a lot going on. And this was, you know, still a vibrant time. There was downtown on weekends, there was the Stuyvesant Casino in…

not much more than a glorified messenger but I got to meet a lot of people and actually was talked into running for office at the American Newspaper Guild, a pretty left wing thing. I was a Wallace — Henry Wallace was running for president. That was that famous election when Truman — Truman and Dewey. And it was a great experience because I was working at Time Inc. I was at a nerve center there on election night, which was a studio where they were broadcasting, and there was a guy named H.V. Kaltenborn, who was —…
